Top autumn walks as leaves expected to be more vibrant

The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve.

Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution.

Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it."

There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows.

Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting".

"In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations.

"You can see the Milky Way - it really is fantastic."

Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop.

The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season.

In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book".

The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park.

Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down.

"We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend."

The growing popularity of the festival meant that many events sold out before the opening day.

articles.body: Lee Marvin, who is best known for his work in ‘Paint Your Wagon,' ‘Point Blank,' ‘The Dirty Dozen,' and ‘The Twilight Zone,' bought out his iconic Tucson estate in 1975. The prestigious Catalina Foothills Estate is one of the most iconic spaces in the Hollywood star’s real estate portfolio. The massive 7,261-square-foot property was once home to the iconic star up until his passing in 1987. While the home had remained in his family for years, it was later sold off in 2021, restored, and recently put up on the market again.In 1975, Lee Marvin bought his iconic Tucson estateThe property, according to reports shared online by Homes.com, came under the Oscar-winning actor’s ownership in 1975. Designed by the famous architect Josias Joesler in 1936, it is located at 5055 N. Calle La Vela. The stunning Tucson property was built with classic mud-adobe and masonry stucco that was popular at the time of its construction, while also featuring a courtyard-centered layout with an expansive fountain, exposed beam ceilings, mission-tile porches, and scored concrete floors.In 2021, Lee Marvin’s Tucson property was finally sold for USD 1.825 millionFor four decades, the 4.12-acre property stayed with the Marvin family well after the ‘Point Blank’ actor’s passing. However, in 2021, the space was sold off for USD 1.825 million and underwent major renovations and reconstructions guided by the new owners, who have not been listed anywhere.The property now includes seven bedrooms and six and a half bathrooms, including the main residence and guest quarters. The kitchen and dining area were fully renovated after it was sold and were turned into a professional chef’s kitchen. The space now features honed marble surfaces, custom cabinetry, Sub-Zero refrigeration, and a Wolf gas range. The space also has a spacious living room, den, and primary suite, all of which have four fireplaces distributed throughout them.One of the specialties of the primary suite of Marvin’s former property includes vaulted/cathedral ceilings, a personal wet bar, double vanity, soaking tub, and custom walk-in closet space. Following its renovations, a lot of features were added and improved. These included a separate detached guest house, along with a studio room, and a 3-car detached garage. Lastly, the vast property also has a lot of outdoor features, including a private swimming pool, tennis court, custom pavers, and natural desert landscaping, which offer the residents stunning and panoramic views of the Catalina Mountains.Lee Marvin’s former property has now come back on the market for USD 5.75 millionOn the listing website Trulia, it was revealed that the property, which belonged to Lee Marvin and was his beloved home until his passing, is now back on the market. It has been listed for sale at the asking price of USD 5.75 million. As of right now, the property is still on the market for sale.Who is Lee Marvin?Born on February 19, 1921, Lee Marvin was one of the most famous stars of his time in the Hollywood industry and was best known for his ‘tough guy’ roles. His career spanned from 1951 to 1986, during which time he worked on more than 130 feature films, as well as TV shows. Before he became an acting icon, Marvin was enlisted in the US Marine Corps during World War II. He served as a scout sniper in the Pacific Theater and was severely wounded in the Battle of Saipan, earning a Purple Heart. articles.body: Ha sido una de las imágenes más virales de las últimas horas. Sin venir a cuento, los espectadores de ‘El sótano Club’ de TEN, vieron como su presentadora, Alba Carrillo, abandonaba rápidamente el plató ante la mirada atónita, preocupada e incómoda de los contertulios. No solo lo hacía de manera improvisada, sino que se mostraba altamente afectada por lo ocurrido. Momentos después, las redes sociales se inundaban con preguntas al respecto de los motivos que han derivado en que Carrillo abandone de esta manera el programa de TEN. Todos se calmaron cuando esta aparecía horas después en el estreno del nuevo canal de television, La Séptima, donde ya se conoce que colaborará como presentadora de programas del canal. En esta presentación, Carrillo parecía estar completamente recompuesta del sofoco que horas antes había protagonizado en ‘El sótano Club’. Ahora, todo parece indicar que esta emoción de la presentadora podría estar ligada a la despedida de la casa que la acogió durante tanto tiempo, ya que este viernes, 16 de octubre, iba a ser su último día como trabajadora para TEN TV, pero finalmente, el programa se ha cancelado. Y es que fue la propia presentadora la que comunicó, en el acto de presentación de La Séptima, los motivos que habían derivado en que esta saliese emocionada del programa, destacando que prefería estar al 100% en un programa y no a medias en dos espacios. La propia cuenta de TEN TV ha anunciado mediante un comunicado en sus redes sociales que hay un inminente “cambio de programación” y que “necesitamos algo de tiempo para trabajar en ellos”, refiriendose a los cambios que se van a producir en el espacio. articles.title: 'The film of the year': Critics rave about Nathan Fielder's 'masterpiece' Elizabeth Holmes movie
articles.summary: Filmed largely in secret, "You Can See Everything" takes viewers inside the life of the Theranos founder before prison.
articles.body:
Nathan Fielder's new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is being hailed by critics as one of the year's best movies.

You Can See Everything , in theaters now, follows the Theranos founder in the weeks leading up to her 2023 imprisonment and the years that followed, after she was convicted of defrauding investors in her blood-testing startup.

One critic said it should be considered alongside the documentary form's "all-time greats."

The film was made largely in secret over nearly four years, with its existence only revealed when it premiered at a surprise screening at the Telluride Film Festival in September.

Fielder, best known for the TV shows Nathan for You and The Rehearsal , has built a career around awkward encounters and elaborate social experiments. The new film was co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, who made the recent Robert Pattinson movie Primetime .

Oppenheim was reluctant to reveal much about the film ahead of its release, telling People , "I don't want to say anything that can skew people's perception of it because I feel like it's one of those movies that the more clean slate you are, the better."

While the documentary has received overwhelmingly positive reviews, critics haven't agreed on everything. Here's what they liked about You Can See Everything — and where they felt it fell short.

What did critics like about 'You Can See Everything'?

You Can See Everything has received near-universal praise, making it one of the year's best-reviewed movies so far.

The Daily Beast called the film an "all-time great mind-melter," with its critic Nick Schager adding, "It's not just the film of the year — it's a documentary that stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the form's all-time greats." Similarly, Vulture called it "the movie of the year" and suggested Holmes was "one of the greatest doc subjects of all time."

The Guardian 's five-star review hailed the movie as a "modern masterpiece of deceit" that lives up to the hype, adding that it is "somehow more shocking, twistier, thornier and revealing than billed."

Fielder is known for blurring the lines between reality and performance, and other reviews suggest the film takes a similarly unconventional approach. Variety called it "just about the furthest thing from a 'pure' documentary you've ever seen," while the Los Angeles Times said it was "far stranger than a conventional documentary."

TheWrap argued that the film "uncovers complex new layers to the Holmes saga," while praising it for transcending the documentary form and being "impossibly involving" — a "documentary to end all documentaries."

Deadline 's critic, Pete Hammond, said it was "unlike any I have ever seen" due to the level of access given to the subjects. Vanity Fair said it was "full of unexpected twists and turns and shocking reveals," with Fielder and Oppenheim having "incredible access" to Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans.

The A.V. Club called it "a stunning reevaluation of what documentaries are capable of," adding, "It's a wild ride, filled with more twists and turns than your average thriller."

What didn't critics like about 'You Can See Everything'?

Despite the glowing reviews, some critics had reservations about the documentary's nearly three-hour runtime and Fielder's treatment of Holmes.

The Washington Post 's Shane O'Neill acknowledged that the film needs its lengthy runtime, but said it "doesn't fly by." "Even for the most hardcore cringe aficionado, it's a tough watch," he wrote, adding that by the second hour, he had developed a stomachache from the discomfort of watching it.

O'Neill warned that viewers unimpressed by the trailer were "in for a long night," though he ultimately called the film a masterpiece.

The New Yorker 's Richard Brody questioned Fielder's treatment of Holmes, arguing that his confrontational style gives his work "an air of cruelty." Brody pointed to Fielder's "sarcastic" exchanges with Holmes, including moments when he "embarrasses" her in front of her parents.

Brody also criticized the film's editing, arguing that it "precludes the tension of continuous unfoldings." Nevertheless, he praised the finished documentary as "strangely, poetically, poignantly beautiful."

The trailer shows Fielder arriving at Holmes and Evans's home with a suitcase, ready to move in while filming the couple. "Does any part of you worry about me being here 24/7?" Fielder asks Holmes, to which she replies, "I don't think so."

"Well, what if I see something that makes you look bad?" he asks. Holmes smiles but does not answer.

Fielder asks Evans whether he was worried Holmes was "scamming" him when they first met. "A hundred percent, but what did she have to gain from me?" Evans replies.

"Well, isn't your family rich?" Fielder asks. "Yeah," says Evans, an heir to a hotel group. "I think there are a lot of different levels of wealth." Evans adds that he has "never" suspected Holmes of lying to him.

Fielder tells Holmes directly that he has a "weird feeling there's some things I'm not seeing." "It's because I don't have anything to hide," she replies.

The trailer ends with Holmes saying, "It took me a really long time to be OK with letting someone see me cry." A single tear then rolls down her cheek.
